kurz: How a dozen contract types that go by the name of bond can be sorted with three questions: who the debtor is and where the creditor stands on the seniority ladder, how the coupon is defined, and in which currency the bond is denominated.

bloecke.md:
“Bond” refers to a type of contract, not a single product. Valuation follows the same present value calculation for every design. The price is the sum of all future payments, each discounted to today. From one design to the next, the only things that change are which payments these are and who makes them under what conditions.

The entire market can therefore be sorted with three questions:

1. Who the debtor is and where the creditor stands on the seniority ladder determines the default risk.
2. How the coupon is defined (fixed, floating, indexed or no coupon) determines the interest rate risk.
3. The currency in which the bond is denominated often matters more than the first two points combined.

Everything else consists of embedded rights such as conversion, calls and loss triggers.

bloecke.titel: Types of bonds and how they differ
zeilen: Maturity ladder from 12 months to 30 years
Cover pool with priority in insolvency

bloecke.md:
## Government bonds as the benchmark

The German federal government issues bonds across a whole ladder of maturities. Bubills run for up to twelve months and carry no coupon, Federal Treasury notes (Schätze) run for two years, Federal notes (Bobls) for five years and Federal bonds in the narrower sense (Bundesanleihen) for seven to thirty years. In addition there are green twin bonds, which exactly match a conventional bond in their terms and maturity, and inflation-linked securities, whose new issuance was discontinued at the end of 2023.

On 18 September 2026, German federal securities with a remaining maturity of two years yielded 3.24%, those with five years 3.30%, ten years 3.52% and thirty years 3.83%. The federal government therefore pays a different interest rate for each maturity.

An Italian government bond is not a foreign currency bond, because it is also denominated in euros. Its yield difference from the German federal bond consists only of the country's credit risk and a liquidity premium. With a US Treasury, by contrast, the exchange rate is added as a further risk.

## Pfandbriefe as a German speciality

The Pfandbrief (German covered bond) is the only widespread type of bond in which a creditor has two independent pools of assets to claim against. First, the creditor has an ordinary claim against the issuing bank. Second, the creditor has a statutory preferential right to a ring-fenced [[Cover pool|cover pool]] of mortgage loans, public sector loans or ship and aircraft financing. If the bank becomes insolvent, this pool does not become part of the insolvency estate. A cover pool administrator (Sachwalter) continues to manage it and services the Pfandbriefe as scheduled.

Under Section 4 PfandBG (Pfandbrief Act), the present value of the cover assets must exceed the present value of the covered liabilities by at least 2%. The Act also specifies what this safeguarding overcollateralisation (sichernde Überdeckung) may consist of, essentially government bonds, central bank balances and balances at banks of the highest credit quality. This is what the strikingly low yield spreads of these securities are based on.

At the end of 2025, German Pfandbriefe with a volume of €410.9 billion were outstanding. In the same year, around €66.8 billion of new issues were added. It is often said that no Pfandbrief has ever defaulted since the instrument was introduced. This lesson does not adopt that claim, because there is no first-hand evidence for it. What is documented is the legal structure, and it is the stronger argument.

bloecke.md:
## Corporate bonds and the seniority ladder

A corporate bond pays more than a government bond because it can default. Within a single issuer there is also a whole ladder of securities that differ only in who loses first if things go wrong. For banks, this ladder has been particularly finely graded since the regulation introduced after 2014. The levels are explicitly named in the prospectus: covered, senior preferred, senior non-preferred, Tier 2 and Additional Tier 1.

The most junior debt tiers bear losses even before insolvency. With an AT1 bond, the coupon can be cancelled or the capital written off entirely while the bank continues to operate and its branches stay open. The trigger is a capital ratio or a decision by the authorities, not an insolvency court.

bloecke.titel: A bank's order of loss absorption
bloecke.unter: From top to bottom the position becomes safer and the coupon smaller; the higher spread further up compensates for the higher risk of loss.

bloecke.md:
In the emergency takeover of Credit Suisse by UBS on 19 March 2023, AT1 bonds worth CHF 16 billion were written off in full. Shareholders, by contrast, still received UBS shares worth around CHF 3 billion. The usual order, in which equity bears losses first and debt afterwards, was thus reversed. The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority FINMA based the write-off on the bond terms and on Swiss emergency law. In October 2025, the Swiss Federal Administrative Court ruled that the contractual trigger had not occurred and that the emergency law did not provide a sufficient legal basis either. The ruling is not final, because FINMA and UBS have appealed to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court. Until that court decides, the bonds remain written off.

Buyers of subordinated bonds acquire rights under the specific bond terms, not under a general rule. What the terms stipulate about triggers, coupon cancellation and write-downs is therefore more important than the position in the theoretical ranking.

## Convertible bonds

A convertible bond gives the creditor the right to exchange the security for a fixed number of the issuer's shares instead of being repaid. This number is the face value divided by the conversion price. At issue, the conversion price is deliberately set above the share price; the difference is called the [[Conversion premium|conversion premium]].

As long as the share stays below the conversion price, the security behaves like a bond and is repaid at face value. If the share rises above it, the security participates in the price increase. The investor pays for this asymmetric distribution of opportunity and risk with a considerably lower coupon. The price of the option is therefore the interest forgone. Two points are regularly overlooked. The bond floor, that is, the value of the security as a pure bond, is only as robust as the issuer's creditworthiness and often gives way just when the share is falling too. With a mandatory convertible, conversion at maturity is also compulsory, so there is no bond floor. In 2008 the Swiss Confederation subscribed to such a mandatory convertible from UBS for six billion Swiss francs with a term of thirty months.

Assume a convertible bond with a face value of €1,000, a coupon of 1.0%, a term of five years and a conversion price of €50. At issue the share is at €40. An ordinary bond from the same issuer pays 4.0%.

- The conversion ratio is 1,000 ÷ 50 = 20 shares.
- The conversion premium is (50 − 40) ÷ 40 = 25%.
- The interest forgone is 3.0 percentage points × 5 years × €1,000 = €150 (calculated without compound interest).

For the convertible to pay off compared with the ordinary bond, the 20 shares must be worth at least €1,150 at the end. That corresponds to a share price of €57.50, around 44% above the price at issue.

If the share is at €52 at maturity, for example, conversion is in the money (20 × 52 = €1,040). However, the gain of €40 does not cover the €150 of interest forgone. The investor is therefore €110 worse off than with the ordinary bond.

## Three types of coupon

A **zero-coupon** bond pays no current interest. The entire return comes from the gap between the purchase price and the face value. At a market yield of 3.52%, a ten-year security with a face value of €100 costs €70.76 today. One advantage is that there is no reinvestment risk and the final amount is known exactly at the time of purchase. For tax purposes, the entire return only arises at maturity and is then taxed at 26.375%. This amounts to a tax deferral, but it also has a drawback. For nine years the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 goes unused, and in the tenth year it is nowhere near enough.

With a **floating-rate note**, the coupon is reset regularly, usually as a reference rate plus a fixed margin. The 3-month Euribor stood at 2.633% on 17 September 2026. A floating-rate note with a margin of 0.8 percentage points then pays around 3.43% for the current quarter. Because the coupon adjusts, the price stays close to 100 and interest rate sensitivity is almost zero. The credit risk, however, remains. If creditworthiness deteriorates, the price of a floating-rate note falls too. If the central bank cuts interest rates, the income falls immediately as well, with no price gain to offset it.

With an **inflation-linked bond**, the face value, and therefore the coupon calculated on it, is linked to a consumer price index, for euro securities usually the HICP excluding tobacco. The investor receives a real return, and the issuer bears the risk of unexpected inflation. German securities of this kind still exist, but no new ones are being added. The issuance of inflation-linked German federal securities was discontinued at the end of 2023. At that time four bonds totalling more than €66 billion were outstanding; in September 2026 three remain, totalling €47.05 billion and maturing in 2030, 2033 and 2046. At maturity, deflation protection applies, so at least the original face value is repaid.

The 2.9% value is the German annual rate for August 2026 and serves only as a guide, because the break-even rate refers to the US market and a ten-year average.

punkte: It secures a real return, that is, purchasing power plus a premium, regardless of the price level.
It protects against inflation that nobody expected and that hurts investors in ordinary bonds.
Through the break-even rate it shows what inflation the market is pricing in, and so provides a measure that does not otherwise exist.
For German securities, repayment cannot fall below the original face value.
It only beats an ordinary bond if inflation is above the break-even rate.
It does not protect against rising real interest rates, because an indexed security also loses value when the real yield rises.
It follows the average of a basket of goods and does not reflect your personal inflation rate.
It is not tax-free, because the inflation compensation from indexation also counts as taxable income.

bloecke.md:
## Foreign currency bonds and exchange rate risk

On 17 September 2026 the ten-year US Treasury yielded 4.94%, the German federal bond of the same maturity 3.55%. The difference of 1.39 percentage points looks like a premium that you can simply pocket. It is not such a premium, because the interest rate differential and the forward exchange rate are linked through covered interest parity. An investor who hedges the currency until maturity pays roughly this difference for the hedge and ends up earning approximately the euro interest rate again. In practice, a rolling hedge over a few months is usual. Its cost depends on the gap between the short-term interest rates of the two currencies, so the hedged return can differ from the ten-year euro interest rate.

Without a hedge, the higher yield is not an additional return, because the investor then holds an open exchange rate risk alongside the bond. In the defensive part of a portfolio, its fluctuation is regularly greater than interest rate and credit risk combined. For this part of your assets, the currency-hedged version is therefore the rule.

## SME bonds (Mittelstandsanleihen)

Between 2010 and 2014, several German stock exchanges set up their own segments for bonds of small and medium-sized enterprises, including Bondm in Stuttgart, the Entry Standard for bonds in Frankfurt and m:access in Munich. The issues were typically between €15 million and €150 million, ran for about five years and offered a spread of up to six percentage points over large industrial bonds of the same maturity. Investors thereby bought a combination of four weaknesses:

- The ratings meant little. They often came from small agencies, were paid for by the issuer itself and did not use a comparable scale.
- Protective clauses (covenants) of the kind that institutional creditors insist on were largely absent.
- There was a lack of liquidity. Investors who wanted to sell could find no buyer if it came to it, especially not after bad news.
- Private investors were the only lenders to companies that had already been turned down by banks.

A typical example is German Pellets. The company had issued bonds and profit participation rights (Genussrechte) with a face value of more than €270 million, subscribed by at least 17,000 investors in Germany. The profit participation rights offered 8% profit-dependent interest with a minimum subscription of €2,500. In February 2016 its refinancing was no longer secure, and investors had to reckon with a total loss.

This lesson does not give a default rate for the segment as a whole, because there is no first-hand evidence for one. What is documented are the individual cases and the fact that the segments no longer exist in their former form.

A security pays 7.0% while the market pays 4.0% for comparable maturities. The extra return of 3.0 percentage points is the price for a higher default risk. With a recovery rate of 40%, each default costs 60% of the amount invested. At an annual probability of default of 3.0 ÷ 0.6 = 5%, the spread is used up on paper. If the default rate is higher, the investor does worse than with a security paying the market rate.

With any high coupon, you should therefore check what default rate is priced in and whether you consider it too high or too low.

bloecke.titel: Identifying the design in the prospectus
bloecke.md:
1. The prospectus states the ranking under “Status” or “Ranking in insolvency”, as senior, subordinated or covered. For bank bonds, search specifically for “preferred” and “non-preferred”.
2. For the coupon, the wording is “fixed interest rate”, “floating interest rate, reference rate Euribor or €STR plus margin” or “index-linked interest rate”.
3. Special rights include call dates, conversion rights and loss triggers. A call right lies with the issuer. The issuer exercises it when it benefits the issuer, which means when it harms the investor.
4. For corporate bonds, a minimum denomination of €100,000 is common. Where it applies, the security is not intended for private investors, and the disclosure requirements are correspondingly lower.

Many corporate bonds and almost all subordinated bonds give the issuer the right to call them on fixed dates. The issuer uses this right when it can refinance more cheaply, that is, after interest rates have fallen or its creditworthiness has improved.

For the creditor, this limits the potential price gain. In the very situation in which the bond's price would rise, the creditor instead gets 100 back and has to reinvest at the new, lower rates. If interest rates rise, the bond is not called, and the creditor remains in the security until maturity.

This is why, for callable securities, the **yield to first call date** is quoted alongside the yield to maturity. The lower of the two figures is the prudent assumption.

mitnehmen: Every type of bond can be classified with three questions about debtor and ranking, coupon and currency; the present value calculation behind it is the same for all designs.

The Pfandbrief is doubly secured, by the claim against the bank and by a statutory preferential right to a separate cover pool with at least 2% overcollateralisation on a present value basis under Section 4 PfandBG; at the end of 2025, €410.9 billion was outstanding.

With subordinated debt and AT1, loss absorption begins before insolvency, because capital can be written off while the bank continues to operate, and with AT1 coupons can also be cancelled. Credit Suisse in 2023 also showed that shareholders do not always bear losses before creditors.

Convertible bonds cost coupon income and are only the better choice once the share exceeds the conversion price plus the entire interest forgone, in the example around 44% above the share price at issue.

Inflation-linked bonds only pay off if inflation is above the break-even inflation rate priced in (2.33% in the US in September 2026); the yardstick is therefore the market's expectation, not zero. No new German securities of this kind have been issued since the end of 2023.

begriffe.text: Pool of mortgage or public sector loans, ring-fenced by law, that secures a Pfandbrief in addition to the bank's liability. If the bank becomes insolvent, it does not become part of the insolvency estate. Section 4 PfandBG (Pfandbrief Act) requires overcollateralisation of at least 2% on a present value basis.

Bond that, in insolvency, is only paid after all other creditors. Banks have graded forms (Tier 2, AT1) whose capital can be written off without insolvency. Only with AT1 can the bank also cancel coupons.

Bond with the right to receive a fixed number of the issuer's shares instead of repayment. The coupon is well below that of an ordinary bond from the same debtor. This interest forgone is the price of the embedded option.

Bond with a floating coupon that is reset periodically as a reference rate (such as 3-month Euribor or €STR) plus a fixed margin. The price stays close to 100, and interest rate risk is almost zero. The credit risk, however, remains unchanged.

Difference between the yield on a nominal bond and that on an inflation-linked bond of the same maturity. It indicates the average inflation the market is already pricing in and is the threshold above which the indexed security pays off.

Percentage gap between a convertible bond's conversion price and the share price at issue. It determines how far the share must rise before the conversion right has intrinsic value, that is, before conversion yields more than repayment. The right has time value even before that.
